sections.title: 1.1 Characteristics of Living Organisms
sections.content:
Biology is the study of life and living organisms. To distinguish between a living entity (like a goat, a mango tree, or a bacterium) and a non-living object (like a stone or a smartphone), biologists use a specific set of life processes known as the characteristics of living organisms.
An easy mnemonic widely used by Nigerian students to remember these characteristics is MR NIGER D:
M — Movement
R — Respiration
N — Nutrition
I — Irritability (Sensitivity)
G — Growth
E — Excretion
R — Reproduction
D — Death / Adaptation

1. Movement

Movement is the ability of an organism to change its position or the position of parts of its body.Animals: Move their entire body from one place to another (known as locomotion) in search of food, mates, or shelter, or to escape predators (e.g., a dog running or a fish swimming in the Niger River).Plants: Do not show locomotion; instead, they display curvature movements or growth movements in response to stimuli (e.g., roots growing toward water or shoot tips bending toward sunlight).

2. Respiration

Respiration is the chemical breakdown of organic food molecules (usually glucose) inside living cells to release energy stored in the form of Adenosine Triphosphate ($ATP$). $$\text{Glucose} + \text{Oxygen} \longrightarrow \text{Carbon Dioxide} + \text{Water} + \text{Energy } (ATP)$$Energy released is used for all cellular activities such as growth, active transport, and movement.

3. Nutrition

Nutrition is the process by which living organisms obtain and assimilate food nutrients required for energy, growth, and tissue repair.Autotrophic Nutrition: Organisms synthesize their own organic food from simple inorganic substances using light energy (e.g., green plants via photosynthesis).Heterotrophic Nutrition: Organisms obtain ready-made organic food by feeding on other organisms (e.g., humans eating eba and egusi soup, fungi absorbing nutrients from decaying cassava).

4. Irritability (Sensitivity)

Irritability is the ability of an organism to detect changes in its internal or external environment (called stimuli) and respond appropriately to them.Example: A person quickly pulling their hand away from a hot pot, or the leaves of the "touch-me-not" plant (Mimosa pudica) folding when touched.

5. Growth

Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in the size, dry mass, complexity, and number of cells of an organism. Growth in animals is limited/determinate (stops at maturity), whereas growth in plants is unlimited/indeterminate (continues throughout life at apical meristems).

6. Excretion

Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products, toxic substances, and substances in excess of requirements from the body of an organism.Metabolic wastes in humans include urea, carbon dioxide, and uric acid.Crucial JAMB Distinction: Excretion is NOT egestive defecation! Defecation is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food matter through the anus, whereas excretion involves chemical wastes produced inside cells during metabolism.

7. Reproduction

Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce new offspring of their own kind, ensuring the continuity of the species and preventing extinction.Asexual Reproduction: Involves a single parent without gamete fusion (e.g., binary fission in Amoeba).Sexual Reproduction: Involves two parents producing male and female gametes that fuse during fertilization (e.g., flowering plants and mammals).8. Adaptation and DeathAdaptation: The possession of special structural, physiological, or behavioral features that enable an organism to survive and reproduce successfully in its specific environment (e.g., cactus spines reducing water loss in arid Northern Nigeria).Death: The ultimate termination of all biological functions and metabolic activities sustaining a living organism.

<mark> JAMB Exam Focus:

JAMB frequently tests the distinction between excretion (removal of metabolic waste like urea and $CO_2$) and egestion/defecation (removal of undigested food feces).Questions often ask candidates to identify features that prove a entity is living or non-living (e.g., viruses act as non-living crystals outside host cells, but reproduce as living entities inside host cells). </mark>

sections.title: 1.2 Cell Structure and Functions of Cell Components
sections.content:
A cell is defined as the basic structural, functional, and organizational unit of all living organisms. All living organisms are made up of either a single cell (unicellular) or many cells (multicellular).

Generalized Structure of Plant and Animal Cells

Both plant and animal cells share basic protoplasmic components, but they possess distinct structural differences adapted to their modes of life.

Detailed Comparison Between Plant and Animal Cells

1. Cell Wall
Plant Cell: Present (rigid outer wall composed of cellulose).

Animal Cell: Absent (bounded only by the flexible cell membrane).

2. Cell Shape
Plant Cell: Fixed, rigid, and definite rectangular shape.

Animal Cell: Flexible, irregular, and variable shape.

3. Chloroplasts (Plastids)
Plant Cell: Present (contains green chlorophyll pigment for photosynthesis).

Animal Cell: Completely absent.

4. Vacuole
Plant Cell: One single, large, central, and permanent vacuole.

Animal Cell: Small, numerous, temporary vacuoles (or completely absent).

5. Centrosome / Centrioles
Plant Cell: Absent (except in certain lower plant forms).

Animal Cell: Present (essential for spindle fiber formation during cell division).

6. Carbohydrate Storage
Plant Cell: Excess carbohydrates stored as Starch grains.

Animal Cell: Excess carbohydrates stored as Glycogen granules.

7. Cytoplasm Distribution
Plant Cell: Confined to a thin layer pushed to the periphery by the large central vacuole.

Animal Cell: Evenly distributed throughout the entire interior cavity of the cell.
1. Cell Wall

Found In: Plant Cells Only

Structure: Rigid, non-living outer boundary composed of cellulose.

Function: Provides mechanical support, tensile strength, and rigidity to give plant cells a definite shape.

2. Cell (Plasma) Membrane

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Selectively permeable, semi-fluid bilayer composed of phospholipids and proteins.

Function: Regulates the osmotic balance and controls the selective entry and exit of substances.

3. Cytoplasm

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Jelly-like fluid matrix containing enzymes, mineral salts, and suspended organelles.

Function: Acts as the primary medium for metabolic chemical reactions and glycolysis.

4. Nucleus

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Double-membrane organelle bounded by a porous nuclear envelope containing chromosomes (DNA).

Function: Directs cellular metabolic activities and carries hereditary genetic information.

5. Nucleolus

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Dense, non-membrane spherical body located inside the nucleoplasm.

Function: Synthesizes ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and coordinates ribosome assembly.

6. Mitochondrion

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Rod-shaped organelle with a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into cristae.

Function: The "powerhouse of the cell" — executes aerobic respiration to generate ATP energy.


7. Chloroplast

Found In: Plant Cells Only

Structure: Double-membrane plastid containing stacked thylakoids (grana) embedded in stroma with green chlorophyll.

Function: Site of photosynthesis, trapping solar radiant energy to manufacture glucose.

8. Ribosome

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Minute, non-membrane granules found freely suspended or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

Function: Responsible for cellular protein synthesis and polypeptide translation.

9. Endoplasmic Reticulum 

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Network of interconnected membranous tubules and sacs extending throughout the cytoplasm.

Function:

Rough ER (studded with ribosomes): Synthesizes and transports proteins.

Smooth ER (lacks ribosomes): Synthesizes lipids, metabolizes carbohydrates, and detoxifies chemicals.

10. Golgi Apparatus (Dictyosome)

Found In: Both Plant and Animal Cells

Structure: Stacks of parallel, flattened, membrane-bound sacs known as cisternae.

Function: Modifies, concentrates, packages, and secretes cellular proteins and glycoproteins.

11. Vacuole

Found In: Both (Distinct structural differences)

Structure: Fluid-filled sac enclosed by a selectively permeable membrane (tonoplast).

Function:

In Plants: Single, large, and permanent; maintains cellular turgor pressure and stores sap.

In Animals: Small, temporary, and contractile/phagocytic (regulates excretion and pinocytosis).

12. Lysosome

Found In: Mainly Animal Cells

Structure: Single membrane-bound vesicle containing concentrated hydrolytic and digestive enzymes.

Function: Acts as the "suicide bag" — breaks down damaged organelles, macromolecules, and ingested pathogens via autophagy.

13. Centrosome (Centrioles)

Found In: Animal Cells Only

Structure: Pair of perpendicular, non-membrane cylindrical structures composed of nine microtubule triplets.

Function: Organizes spindle fibers to separate sister chromatids during mitotic and meiotic cell division.
